I'm Andrew. I go by PK online.

Hi, I’m Andrew—a computer science student at California State University, Long Beach who enjoys building things that make everyday life a little easier. Working in warehouse operations at STRAYE sparked my interest in turning frustrating, repetitive tasks into useful software. I’m still learning, experimenting, and figuring things out, and this website is where I share what I’m building along the way. Outside of school and work, you’ll usually find me gaming, exploring somewhere new with my camera, enjoying a matcha, or spending time with my dog, Suki. Thanks for stopping by—I’m glad you’re here. Check out my GitHub here.

Warehouse picking pipeline

A practical automation project for the warehouse workflow at STRAYE.

The problem
Order exports need to become clear, organized instructions for the people picking and packing them.
The approach
A Python workflow transforms CSV data into picking PDFs, organizing orders by warehouse zones and separating different picking needs.

Readable output, consistent ordering, and less repetitive spreadsheet work.

The notebook

Working notes on code,
systems, and learning.

AutomationDraft

Start with the repeatable part.

On finding a useful first thing to automate.

Read ↗

A good starting point for automation is a task someone already repeats: opening an export, rearranging columns, sorting rows, and making the same document again.

Before writing the script, map the process. What comes in? What decisions happen? What should the final output look like? The exceptions matter just as much as the normal path.

The useful result is a workflow someone can trust. A readable picking list, a clear error message, and a predictable file format can matter more than adding another feature.

LearningDraft

Understand the layer underneath.

A habit for making technical ideas stick.

Read ↗

When a tool makes something easy, there is still value in understanding the work it hides. An API call has a request and a response. A program becomes instructions. A database query expresses a question about data.

One way to learn is to follow a small example through the whole process. Identify the input, trace what happens to it, and explain the output without skipping the unfamiliar steps.

Then change one thing. Predict what will happen before running it. The difference between the prediction and the result is often the most useful part of the exercise.

An open notebook. Room for ideas that are still taking shape.
